table.caption: Hours of labor needed to make one unit in two invented countries (invented data for practice)

items.q: A producer has a comparative advantage in a good when it can make that good
options: in a larger amount than another producer
with more workers than the other producer uses
at a lower opportunity cost
at a higher price than another producer

why.correct: Comparative advantage is about opportunity cost: what you give up to make one more unit.
options: Making more with the same resources is absolute advantage.
Using more workers says nothing about what each unit costs in other goods.
Right: lower opportunity cost.
Price is not how either advantage is defined.

items.q: What is Fenwick's opportunity cost of one table, in chairs?

why.correct: Fenwick gives up 12 chairs to make 6 tables: $\frac{12}{6} = 2$ chairs per table.

mistakes.why: That is the cost of a CHAIR in tables. For a table, put the chairs given up (12) on top and the tables gained (6) below.

items.q: What is Garnet's opportunity cost of one chair, in tables?

why.correct: Garnet gives up 2 tables to make 8 chairs: $\frac{2}{8} = 0.25$ table per chair.

mistakes.why: That is the cost of a TABLE in chairs. For a chair, divide the tables given up (2) by the chairs gained (8).

items.q: Which workshop has the absolute advantage in making chairs?
options: Fenwick, because it can make 12 a day to Garnet's 8
Garnet, because a chair costs it just a quarter of a table
Garnet, because it makes fewer tables
Neither, because both can make chairs

why.correct: Absolute advantage compares amounts made: Fenwick makes 12 chairs a day, Garnet 8.
options: Right: more output with the same day of work.
A lower opportunity cost is comparative advantage, not absolute.
Making fewer tables is not an advantage in chairs.
Both can make chairs, but Fenwick makes more.

items.q: Which workshop has the comparative advantage in tables, and why?
options: Garnet: a table costs it 4 chairs, Fenwick 2
Fenwick: it makes 6 tables to Garnet's 2
Neither: Fenwick is better at both goods
Fenwick: a table costs it 2 chairs, Garnet 4

why.correct: Compare opportunity costs of a table: 2 chairs for Fenwick, 4 for Garnet. The lower cost wins.
options: The comparative advantage goes to the LOWER cost, which is Fenwick's.
That compares amounts, which is absolute advantage.
Being better at both is absolute advantage; costs still differ, so each has a comparative advantage.
Right: 2 chairs is less than 4.

items.q: Garnet specializes in chairs and Fenwick in tables. Which price for one table, paid in chairs, would benefit both workshops?
options: 1 chair
3 chairs
5 chairs
8 chairs

why.correct: A table costs Fenwick 2 chairs to make and Garnet 4. At 3 chairs per table, Fenwick gets more than 2 for each table it sells and Garnet pays less than 4.
options: At 1 chair, Fenwick gets less than the 2 chairs a table costs it to make.
Right: between 2 and 4.
At 5 chairs, Garnet pays more than the 4 chairs it would give up to make a table itself.
At 8 chairs, Garnet would pay twice its own cost.

items.q: In Corvania, what is the opportunity cost of one bolt of cloth, in bushels of rice?

why.correct: The 4 hours for a bolt of cloth could make $\frac{4}{2} = 2$ bushels of rice instead. With an input table, divide the hours for the good by the hours for the other good.

mistakes.why: That is the output-table rule applied to hours. With hours per unit, divide the hours for cloth (4) by the hours for rice (2).

items.q: Which country has the absolute advantage in both goods?
options: Lumeria, because it needs more hours for each good
Corvania: fewer hours for each good
Corvania in rice and Lumeria in cloth
Neither country

why.correct: With an input table, fewer hours per unit means more output from the same labor. Corvania needs 2 hours for rice (Lumeria 3) and 4 for cloth (Lumeria 9).
options: More hours per unit means LESS output from the same labor.
Right: fewer hours for both.
Corvania uses fewer hours for cloth too.
Corvania uses fewer hours for both goods.

items.q: Which country has the comparative advantage in rice?
options: Corvania: it needs fewer hours for rice
Corvania: 1/2 bolt per bushel, to Lumeria's 1/3
Lumeria: it needs more hours for rice
Lumeria: 1/3 bolt per bushel, to Corvania's 1/2

why.correct: Opportunity cost of a bushel of rice: Corvania 2 ÷ 4 = 1/2 bolt, Lumeria 3 ÷ 9 = 1/3 bolt. Lumeria's is lower.
options: Fewer hours is absolute advantage, not comparative.
The comparative advantage goes to the LOWER cost, Lumeria's 1/3.
Needing more hours is not why; its lower opportunity cost is.
Right: 1/3 is less than 1/2.

items.q: If the two countries specialize by comparative advantage, what will each produce?
options: Corvania cloth and Lumeria rice
Corvania rice and Lumeria cloth
Corvania both goods
Lumeria both goods

why.correct: Cloth costs Corvania 2 bushels of rice and Lumeria 3, so Corvania specializes in cloth. Lumeria has the lower cost of rice.
options: Right: each makes its lower-cost good.
That reverses both comparative advantages.
Specializing in both goods is not possible; each country has a comparative advantage in only one.
Lumeria has the comparative advantage in rice only.

items.q: Fenwick can make 12 chairs or 6 tables a day, or any mix on a straight line between them. Label the axes and the curve of its production possibilities graph.

why.correct: Chairs go on the horizontal axis and Tables on the vertical axis, as drawn, and the straight line is Fenwick's PPC.

items.q: Fenwick specializes in tables and trades some for chairs. It ends up with 6 chairs and 4 tables. Place point C at that combination.

why.correct: On its own line, 6 chairs leaves room for only 3 tables. With 4 tables, point C lies outside Fenwick's PPC: trade lets it consume beyond what it can make alone.

items.q: What does it mean to specialize?
options: To make each good you consume by yourself
To buy most goods from producers in other countries
To focus production on a few goods
To make the good with the highest price

why.correct: Specializing means focusing on what you make at a low opportunity cost and trading for the rest.
options: Making everything yourself is the opposite of specializing.
Buying from others is trade; specializing is about what you make.
Right: focus on a few goods.
Specializing follows opportunity cost, not the highest price.

items.q: Two bakers have the same opportunity cost of a pie: 3 loaves of bread each. What can trade between them do?
options: The faster baker gains and the slower one loses
Both gain, as two producers do from any trade
The slower baker gains the most
Neither gains from trading

why.correct: Gains from trade come from different opportunity costs. With equal costs, there is no price between them that helps one without hurting the other.
options: Speed is absolute advantage; what matters is that the costs are equal.
Gains need different opportunity costs.
With equal costs, neither has a cost advantage to trade on.
Right: equal costs leave no gain.

items.q: A lawyer types faster than her assistant. Why might she still pay the assistant to do her typing?
options: She has the comparative advantage in typing
Her assistant has the absolute advantage in typing
Typing costs her valuable legal work
Typing has no opportunity cost

why.correct: Her opportunity cost of typing is the legal work she gives up, which is high. The assistant gives up much less, so the assistant has the comparative advantage in typing.
options: Her opportunity cost of typing is the higher one, so the assistant has the comparative advantage.
She types faster, so SHE has the absolute advantage.
Right: her opportunity cost of typing is high.
Every hour spent typing gives up some other use.

items.q: A bushel of corn costs Country P 2 bushels of wheat and Country Q 5. Country P specializes in corn. At which prices, in wheat per bushel of corn, would both countries gain? Select all that apply.
options: 3 bushels of wheat
4 bushels of wheat
1 bushel of wheat
6 bushels of wheat

why.correct: Both gain at any price between the two opportunity costs, 2 and 5 bushels of wheat.
options: Right: between 2 and 5.
Right: between 2 and 5.
At 1, P gets less than the 2 bushels of wheat corn costs it.
At 6, Q pays more than the 5 it would give up to grow corn itself.

items.q: Put the steps for showing that two producers gain from trade in order.
options: Find each producer's opportunity cost of each good
Compare costs to find each comparative advantage
Have each specialize in its comparative-advantage good
Trade at a price between the two opportunity costs

why.correct: Costs first, then comparative advantage, then specialization, then terms of trade between the costs.
